On average, Inspector A does not meet the certification bar of 18 correctly classified items.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$
P(X = n) = p^{n}
$$

For side A, $p = 0.75$ and $n = 20$:

$$
P(X = 20)
$$

$$
(0.75)^{20} = 0.003171211939
$$

$$
0.32\%
$$

The claim compares this with $0.2\%$. We got about $0.3171\%$, which is above the cutoff.

So the statement is False.
**B.** → True

The named event covers every admissible count from 18 through 20, not only the single count 18. Those extra counts have positive probability when $0<p<1$, so the event probability is strictly larger than $P(X=18)$.

So the statement is True.
**C.** → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 18 successes out of 20. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 18, 19, \ldots, 20$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$
P(X \ge 18) = \sum_{x = 18}^{20} \binom{20}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{20-x}
$$

A single term $P(X = k)$ would only count “exactly $k$” and would miss the rest of the tail, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two success probabilities $p$.

$$
P(X = 18) = \binom{20}{18} (0.75)^{18} (0.25)^{2}
$$

$$
\binom{20}{18} = \dfrac{20!}{18!(20-18)!}
$$

$$
\dfrac{20!}{18!(2)!} = \dfrac{20 \cdot 19}{1 \cdot 2}
$$

$$
20 \cdot 19 = 380
$$

$$

$$

$$
\binom{20}{18} = 190

$$
(0.75)^{18} = 0.005637710114

(0.25)^{2}

$$

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with success probability $p$. Each trial has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)

$$
\mathrm{Var}(A) = 20 \cdot 0.75 \cdot 0.25
$$

19 \times 0.05 = 0.95
$$

The variance ratio is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{3.75}{0.95} \approx 3.95
$$

.

So the statement is False.
**E.** → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials each with mean $p$:

$$
E[X] = np
$$

$$
E[A] = 20 \cdot 0.75
$$

$$

$$

Compare with the bar $k = 18$: $E[A] = 15$ is below 18.

So the statement is True.
